paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical test for deciding whether two variables are independent. It compares their joint distribution with the distribution obtained by combining their separate marginal distributions. Independence means these descriptions agree. The proposed dependence measure represents both distributions through analytic kernel embeddings and checks their differences at a finite collection of feature locations.

The method chooses these locations to maximize a lower bound on test power: the ability to detect dependence when it is present. This makes feature selection part of the testing procedure. The selected locations also offer an interpretation of the result, highlighting regions where the observed joint behavior differs most from what independence would imply.

The test runs in time linear in sample size, and the authors establish consistency for an appropriate choice of features. On real-world benchmarks, optimized features give performance comparable to the quadratic-time HSIC test and better than competing linear-time and O(n log n) tests. These findings support efficient, interpretable dependence testing without claiming that every feature choice works equally well.
icml-2017-an-adaptive-test-of-independen.tldr: An adaptive independence test selects informative kernel features to detect dependence in linear time and reveal where it occurs.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to divide a graph into clusters using a mathematical representation called lifted multicuts. Its starting point is a characterization of the entire collection of graph decompositions. This gives a common language for reasoning about which clusterings are possible and for searching for a clustering with the lowest specified cost.

One use of this characterization is to understand constraints that require particular elements to belong together or remain separate. These must-join and must-cut requirements define classes of acceptable decompositions. The same perspective also yields insights into metrics for comparing clusterings, connecting the description of individual solutions with ways to measure differences between them.

For optimization, the authors investigate facets of lifted multicut polytopes, geometric structures that represent the problem's feasible choices. They develop efficient separation procedures and incorporate them into a branch-and-cut algorithm for finding minimum-cost lifted multicuts. The contribution therefore combines structural analysis with an optimization method: it explains aspects of the space of graph clusterings and uses that understanding to help search it.
icml-2017-analysis-and-optimization-of-g.tldr: Lifted multicuts provide a framework for analyzing constrained graph clusterings and optimizing them with a branch-and-cut algorithm.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings of a function whose evaluations are expensive. This paper addresses cases where the choices being optimized have a known dependency structure organized as a tree. That structure matters because the search space contains related sequences of decisions, and treating every sequence independently would overlook information they share.

The proposed surrogate model combines independent Gaussian processes with a linear model encoding the tree dependencies. It can transfer information between decision sequences that overlap. A specialized acquisition function then selects what to evaluate through a two-step procedure designed to explore this structured space more effectively.

The authors report two benefits: more efficient exploration and posterior inference that scales more favorably with the number of observations than published Gaussian-process approaches. Experiments cover synthetic tree-structured functions and tuning feedforward neural networks on binary classification datasets, with favorable comparisons to competing methods. The contribution is specifically about exploiting known dependencies, showing how the organization of an optimization domain can inform both its predictive model and its search strategy.
icml-2017-bayesian-optimization-with-tre.tldr: A tree-aware Bayesian optimization model shares information across related decisions to improve search and inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an agent receives rich observations and must use function approximation to guide decisions. The paper introduces contextual decision processes as a framework encompassing most earlier reinforcement-learning settings. Within this framework, it asks what structure makes systematic exploration and learning near-optimal behavior possible with a manageable number of observations.

The central structural measure is Bellman rank. The authors show that low Bellman rank supports tractable learning and that the measure is naturally small in many well-studied models. This shifts attention from the sheer number of distinct contexts to a complexity property that can remain small even when the observation space is large.

The proposed algorithm combines Bellman error minimization with optimistic exploration. For contextual decision processes with low Bellman rank, its sample requirement is polynomial in the relevant parameters and independent of the number of unique contexts. The result supplies a theoretical route to efficient exploration with function approximation. Its guarantee depends on the low-rank structure, rather than applying indiscriminately to every problem with rich observations.
icml-2017-contextual-decision-processes-.tldr: Low Bellman rank enables systematic reinforcement-learning exploration with sample requirements independent of the number of distinct contexts.

paragraphs: Ordinary neural-network training couples the timing of different layers. A layer must wait for later computations and the returning error signal before updating its weights. This paper introduces learned models of future computation so that modules can estimate the information they need locally, reducing this dependency between different parts of the network.

The main application predicts error gradients. A module uses a synthetic gradient in place of the gradient that would arrive through backpropagation, allowing independent and asynchronous updates. The authors demonstrate feedforward networks in which every layer trains asynchronously. They also study recurrent networks, where predicting future gradients extends the time span over which the network can effectively model sequences.

Further demonstrations include a hierarchical recurrent system operating at different timescales. The framework can also predict inputs, allowing modules to become decoupled during both forward computation and backward error propagation. These independently learning networks can then work together as a functioning system. The contribution is a way to reorganize training around learned interfaces, with results across several network arrangements.
icml-2017-decoupled-neural-interfaces-us.tldr: Synthetic gradients let neural-network modules update asynchronously by predicting the error signals they would otherwise wait to receive.

paragraphs: The paper presents a probabilistic model for discovering overlapping communities and predicting links in graph data. Each node can have multiple layers of hidden features or community memberships. This deep organization is intended to capture more complex network structure while making the learned features more interpretable.

The framework also uses information attached to nodes, such as their attributes. A regression component directly conditions the hidden node features on this side information, bringing attributes and graph structure into one model. Through data augmentation, the authors obtain full local conjugacy, enabling an efficient Gibbs sampling procedure with closed-form updates.

Inference cost scales with the number of edges, making the approach attractive for large graphs that are sparse. The model can also be extended to weighted networks whose edges contain counts. The authors report superior link prediction on more complex networks and provide quantitative and qualitative comparisons with existing methods on benchmark datasets. Together, these contributions connect layered community representations, node attributes, and computationally efficient inference within a unified probabilistic framework.
icml-2017-deep-generative-models-for-rel.tldr: A deep probabilistic graph model combines layered community memberships with node attributes for link prediction and interpretable relational modeling.

paragraphs: The paper gives a statistical analysis of DBSCAN as a method for recovering connected high-density regions. Its target is the set of locations where an unknown density is at least a chosen threshold, lambda. Given independent, identically distributed samples, the goal is to estimate the connected components of that set.

The analysis measures geometric estimation error using Hausdorff distance and describes boundary regularity through a parameter beta greater than zero. For data in D-dimensional Euclidean space, the error rate is n^(-1/(2 beta + D)), up to logarithmic factors. This matches known lower bounds to that same qualification, providing a precise statistical justification for the method in this setting.

When observations instead lie on an unknown embedded manifold of dimension d, the rate becomes n^(-1/(2 beta + d max{1, beta})), again up to logarithmic factors. The authors also provide adaptive tuning that attains these rates without prior knowledge of intrinsic dimension, density, or beta. The results connect DBSCAN's recovery accuracy to boundary structure and the dimension on which the data actually lies.
icml-2017-density-level-set-estimation-o.tldr: DBSCAN can recover connected density regions with quantified error rates and adaptive tuning, including when data lies on an unknown manifold.

paragraphs: The paper explains Nesterov's accelerated optimization method through dissipativity, a concept from control theory. The guiding idea is to relate progress in an optimization algorithm to the dissipation of energy in a physical system. This provides an intuitive interpretation while supporting rigorous statements about how quickly the method converges.

A key practical benefit is a systematic way to construct Lyapunov functions, mathematical quantities used to certify progress. The authors show that dissipativity permits their numerical or analytical construction through a small semidefinite program. They introduce supply rate functions that allow the framework to recover known convergence-rate bounds for Nesterov's method.

The approach also certifies linear and sublinear convergence rates across a variety of settings. Its continuous-time formulation connects with research that analyzes optimization algorithms using discretized ordinary differential equations. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and methodological: it links acceleration to energy reasoning and supplies a tractable procedure for building convergence certificates, rather than presenting a new accelerated optimizer.
icml-2017-dissipativity-theory-for-neste.tldr: Dissipativity theory explains Nesterov acceleration through energy dissipation and provides a systematic way to certify convergence rates.

paragraphs: Active search aims to find as many members of a desired class as possible with a limited labeling budget. A useful decision may uncover a target immediately or reveal information that improves later searches. This paper studies that tension while explicitly accounting for how many opportunities to inspect candidates remain.

The authors first establish a hardness result: no polynomial-time policy can achieve a constant-factor approximation to the optimal policy's expected utility in the studied problem. They then propose a computationally efficient policy that considers the entire remaining budget. Its balance between exploration and exploitation changes automatically with that budget, without a separate parameter controlling the tradeoff.

Experiments span drug discovery, materials science, and a citation network. The proposed policy finds significantly more valuable points under the same budget than several existing alternatives, including myopic approximations to the optimal policy. These empirical gains coexist with the theoretical hardness result: the method performs strongly on the evaluated tasks without supplying a general constant-factor approximation guarantee.
icml-2017-efficient-nonmyopic-active-sea.tldr: An efficient active-search policy uses the remaining budget to balance exploration and exploitation, finding more targets in evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies a fairness requirement for reinforcement learning, where an action can change both the environment and future rewards. Its definition says that a learning algorithm must never favor one action over another when the latter has greater long-term discounted reward. Fairness is therefore tied to the actions' future value.

An optimal policy is compatible with this requirement, but learning under it can be difficult. The authors prove that any algorithm satisfying exact fairness must take time exponential in the number of states to obtain a nontrivial approximation to the optimal policy. Compatibility with the eventual best behavior does not by itself make the learning process efficient.

The paper then relaxes the requirement to an approximate notion of fairness and provides a polynomial-time algorithm that is provably fair under that definition. This establishes an exponential separation between exact and approximate fairness. The finding identifies a consequential tradeoff in the stated framework: how strictly fairness is required during learning can fundamentally change the time needed to learn useful behavior.
icml-2017-fairness-in-reinforcement-lear.tldr: Exact reward-based fairness can make reinforcement learning exponentially slow, while an approximate fairness requirement permits polynomial-time learning.

paragraphs: The paper builds a generative image model around recurring patterns in small image patches. It aims to capture both repetition within an image and structure shared across an image collection. The starting point is a variational interpretation of expected patch log-likelihood, or EPLL, using randomly positioned grids of patches.

Earlier EPLL approaches represented patches with a fixed finite mixture of Gaussians. Here, Dirichlet process mixtures let model complexity grow as more images are observed. A hierarchical extension lets images share patch structure while differing in how frequently particular clusters occur. This gives a probabilistic account of image-specific repetition within a shared collection.

The authors derive structured variational inference that creates new patch clusters as needed to represent unfamiliar textures more accurately. On standard denoising benchmarks, the method outperforms EPLL and performs comparably to the state of the art. They also report accurate image inpainting and statistical justifications for common image-processing heuristics. The contribution links an adaptable patch model to both practical restoration results and an interpretation of existing techniques.
icml-2017-from-patches-to-images-a-nonpa.tldr: A hierarchical nonparametric patch model adapts to new textures and captures image repetition, supporting strong denoising and inpainting results.

paragraphs: Deep latent Gaussian models describe high-dimensional observations through hidden Gaussian variables and deep probabilistic structure. The paper examines how to fit these models. Their usual training approach, variational expectation-maximization, approximates maximum marginal likelihood and supplies biased gradient signals. The authors investigate Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative route to learning.

The attraction of MCMC is that it allows a tradeoff between bias and computation. Instead of committing to the usual variational approximation, training uses a sampling-based approach whose computational investment can address approximation bias. This makes the quality of the learning signal and the expense of obtaining it central to the comparison.

The authors find higher held-out likelihoods, sharper generated images, and avoidance of the variational overpruning effect with their MCMC-based approach. These are reported outcomes of the study, rather than universal guarantees for MCMC training. The additional computational overhead is substantial but judged not prohibitive. The results make a case that more expensive inference can offer worthwhile improvements in these deep generative models.
icml-2017-learning-deep-latent-gaussian-.tldr: MCMC-based training improves reported likelihood and image quality for deep latent Gaussian models at a substantial but manageable computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning compact discrete representations, including cluster assignments and hash codes. Deep networks can capture nonlinear patterns and handle large datasets, but their flexibility makes regularization important. A useful representation should preserve relevant information while remaining stable under transformations that an application intends to treat as equivalent.

Information Maximizing Self-Augmented Training, or IMSAT, combines two objectives. Data augmentation encourages an original example and its transformed versions to receive similar predicted representations. At the same time, the method maximizes the information-theoretic dependence between inputs and their discrete representations. Both goals are incorporated into end-to-end training.

The combination matters because stability alone does not express the need for informative representations. IMSAT explicitly asks for both the chosen invariances and a strong connection to the data. Extensive benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art results for clustering and unsupervised hash learning. These findings support the proposed pairing of augmentation-based regularization with information maximization across two tasks that share the need for compact, meaningful discrete outputs.
icml-2017-learning-discrete-representati.tldr: IMSAT learns informative discrete representations by combining augmentation-based consistency with information maximization.

paragraphs: The paper studies graph-based detection of Sybil accounts used to manipulate online social-network services. It begins with the robustness of two existing detectors, SybilRank and Integro. The authors refine their theoretical security guarantees toward more realistic assumptions, making the conditions behind protection part of the analysis.

They then formalize adversarial versions of the detection problem and derive a corresponding optimal attack strategy based on exploiting trust leaks. This identifies a specific weakness within the modeled interaction between attacker and detector. The proposed defense, transductive Sybil ranking or TSR, extends SybilRank and Integro by directly minimizing those trust leaks.

Empirical evaluation considers a variety of attack scenarios on artificially generated and real-world data. TSR shows significant advantages over state-of-the-art competitors in those evaluations. The contribution connects security analysis to algorithm design: a formally studied attack mechanism becomes the quantity the defense tries to reduce. The optimal-attack result belongs to the defined adversarial settings, while the reported practical robustness is supported by the tested scenarios.
icml-2017-minimizing-trust-leaks-for-rob.tldr: Transductive Sybil ranking strengthens graph-based detection by directly minimizing trust leaks identified through adversarial analysis.

paragraphs: Multilevel clustering asks two related questions: how should observations within each group be partitioned, and which groups exhibit similar patterns? The paper addresses these questions together for hierarchically organized data. This joint view matters because local clusters and broader relationships among groups are parts of the same modeling problem.

The authors formulate an optimization problem over several spaces of discrete probability measures, using Wasserstein distances to compare them. They connect this formulation to Wasserstein barycenters, which serve as representative centers for distributions. That connection leads to several variants of the problem with fast optimization algorithms.

The paper establishes consistency properties for estimates of both local and global clusters, giving theoretical support at each level of the hierarchy. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the proposed approach's flexibility and scalability. The contribution is a shared mathematical framework for discovering structure within groups and across groups, together with computational variants and statistical results that address both levels rather than treating them as unrelated clustering tasks.
icml-2017-multilevel-clustering-via-wass.tldr: A Wasserstein-based framework jointly discovers clusters within groups and patterns across groups, with consistency results and fast optimization variants.

paragraphs: The paper considers nonconvex optimization and learning carried out by a network of distributed nodes. The nodes must collectively solve an optimization problem through a distributed procedure. The proposed method, the Proximal Primal-Dual Algorithm or Prox-PDA, supplies a convergence-rate guarantee for this network setting.

The target is first-order stationarity, a condition expressing that first-order information no longer provides a direction of improvement. In a nonconvex problem, this is distinct from identifying a globally optimal solution. The authors establish global sublinear convergence toward the set of first-order stationary solutions, with a rate of O(1/r), where r counts iterations.

This rate quantifies how the algorithm progresses as distributed computation continues. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first distributed nonconvex optimization algorithm with a global rate guarantee. Numerical experiments also demonstrate effectiveness. The main contribution is thus a theoretically controlled distributed procedure for seeking stationary solutions, supported by numerical evidence; the word global in the rate claim should not be read as a guarantee of global optimality.
icml-2017-prox-pda-the-proximal-primal-d.tldr: Prox-PDA enables distributed nonconvex optimization with an O(1/r) convergence rate toward first-order stationary solutions.

paragraphs: In multi-label learning, an example can have several labels, and a recorded zero may mean either absence or missing information. This paper builds a generative framework that explicitly models this ambiguity. A latent factor model represents the binary label matrix, while an exposure model accounts for whether label observations are missing.

The model also connects labels to the available input features. It assumes that an example's low-dimensional label representation is directly conditioned on that example's feature vector. This couples the structure among labels with information about the example, while the exposure component handles uncertainty about what the recorded zeros mean.

Parameter estimation reduces to a sequence of weighted least-squares regression problems that can be solved efficiently and in parallel. Inference also supports online processing through mini-batches, making the framework scalable to large datasets with moderate computational resources. The authors report quantitative and qualitative benchmark comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines explicit treatment of missing labels with an inference procedure built from relatively simple computational steps.
icml-2017-scalable-generative-models-for.tldr: A generative multi-label model distinguishes absent labels from missing observations while supporting efficient parallel and mini-batch inference.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to improve generated sequences according to domain-specific goals while preserving knowledge learned from data and sample diversity. It starts with a recurrent neural network trained by maximum likelihood. That model's distribution over the next token becomes a prior policy describing the behavior that later training should remain close to.

A second recurrent network is trained with reinforcement learning to pursue the desired incentives. Its objective also favors proximity to the prior policy, giving the fine-tuning process an explicit connection to the original data-trained model. The authors derive off-policy reinforcement-learning methods from KL-control to formalize this combination.

The approach is demonstrated on musical melody generation and computational molecular generation. In both applications, the authors report improvements in desired properties and sequence structure while retaining information learned from data. The method matters because it incorporates both specialized rewards and preservation of learned behavior into the training objective. Its reported successes show this balance working in two different sequence-generation domains.
icml-2017-sequence-tutor-conservative-fi.tldr: Sequence Tutor uses KL-control to improve generated sequences through reinforcement learning while staying close to a data-trained prior model.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification with a very large number of labels using a hierarchical predictor. Such predictors depend heavily on how their decision tree is organized. Earlier methods could learn that organization while keeping input features fixed; this work learns the input representation and the hierarchy together.

The proposed objective favors multi-way partitions at tree nodes that are both balanced and easy to separate. Joint learning lets the representations and the predictive structure adapt within the same optimization process. The authors analyze the objective theoretically, establishing a boosting-style property and a bound on classification error.

They also extend the algorithm to conditional density estimation. Empirical evaluation uses text classification for the classification variant and language modeling for the density-estimation variant. Both compare favorably with common baselines in accuracy and running time. The contribution connects the organization of a large output space with the features used to navigate it, and supports that joint design through both theoretical analysis and experiments on the two applications.
icml-2017-simultaneous-learning-of-trees.tldr: Jointly learning input representations and a balanced predictive hierarchy improves reported accuracy and runtime for classification and language modeling.

paragraphs: Temporal sequences can contain patterns operating over different cycles. LSTMs can capture long-range dependencies in time, but they do not explicitly represent how patterns occur across frequencies. The paper introduces State-Frequency Memory, or SFM, to make this frequency structure part of a recurrent network's representation of a sequence.

SFM decomposes remembered dynamics jointly into state and frequency components. This allows the architecture to separate dynamic patterns associated with different frequencies and represent their influence on temporal context. The aim is a finer-grained account of sequence behavior that captures dependencies in both the time and frequency domains.

Evaluations on several temporal modeling tasks show competitive performance, particularly in comparison with state-of-the-art LSTM models. The claim is competitiveness across the reported evaluations, rather than universal superiority over LSTMs. The architectural contribution is the explicit organization of memory by frequency as well as state, providing a way to represent cyclic structure alongside the temporal dependencies that recurrent networks already seek to capture.
icml-2017-state-frequency-memory-recurre.tldr: State-Frequency Memory explicitly separates recurrent dynamics by frequency to model sequence patterns across time cycles.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition represents a high-dimensional array using lower-dimensional structure. The paper observes that spatial and temporal data can have another useful property: adjacent entries often vary smoothly. Its smoothed Tucker decomposition, or STD, incorporates this smoothness alongside the low-dimensional structure that motivates Tucker decomposition.

STD expresses smooth structure using a sum of a few basis functions, reducing the number of parameters needed for the representation. The authors formulate the objective as a convex problem and derive an optimization algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers. The modeling choice and solver are therefore developed together.

The theoretical result is a better error bound under the smoothness assumption. That condition is central: the improvement is justified for data satisfying the assumed smooth structure. Numerical results verify the theoretical finding and the performance of STD. The contribution shows how neighboring-entry relationships can supply additional information beyond low dimensionality, and how that information can be incorporated into a tensor model with a corresponding estimation guarantee.
icml-2017-tensor-decomposition-with-smoo.tldr: Smoothed Tucker decomposition uses basis functions to reduce parameters and achieves a better error bound under a smoothness assumption.

paragraphs: The paper aims to generate plausible sentences while controlling attributes such as sentiment and tense. It seeks latent representations whose parts have designated meanings, so that generation can respond to interpretable controls. The proposed neural model combines a variational autoencoder with attribute discriminators that assess generated text as a whole.

Several components support this learning process: a differentiable approximation to discrete text samples, explicit constraints on independent attribute controls, and collaborative training of the generator and discriminators. The authors also interpret the method as enhancing a variational autoencoder with wake-sleep learning, using generated samples as additional training data.

The model learns interpretable representations even with only word annotations and produces short sentences with desired sentiment and tense attributes. Quantitative experiments use trained classifiers to evaluate sentence and attribute generation, supporting the reported accuracy. The contribution is a framework that builds semantic controls into generative learning, with evidence focused on short sentences and the specified attributes rather than unrestricted control over every aspect of text.
icml-2017-toward-controlled-generation-o.tldr: A variational text generator with attribute discriminators learns interpretable controls for producing short sentences with desired sentiment and tense.

paragraphs: Unitary matrices offer a promising approach to exploding and vanishing gradients, especially in recurrent networks learning long-term correlations. This paper introduces an Efficient Unitary Neural Network architecture, or EUNN. Its design addresses how broadly a network can represent unitary transformations and how much computation that representation requires.

The representation capacity is tunable, ranging from a subspace of SU(N) to the full unitary space. This makes the extent of the available transformations an explicit architectural choice. The authors also report training complexity of O(1) per parameter, a computational property that complements the adjustable representation capacity.

Evaluation covers the copying task, pixel-permuted MNIST digit recognition, and speech prediction on TIMIT. The architecture significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art unitary recurrent networks and LSTMs in final performance, wall-clock training speed, or both. Those alternatives should remain distinct: the abstract does not claim simultaneous gains on every measure in every test. The findings position EUNNs as promising recurrent-model alternatives with flexible capacity and efficient parameterization.
icml-2017-tunable-efficient-unitary-neur.tldr: EUNNs offer tunable unitary representation capacity and efficient training, with reported gains in task performance and/or training speed.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation builds a density estimate from observed data without requiring a fixed parametric form. This paper derives finite-sample bounds on its estimation error for multivariate data under mild assumptions on the density. The bounds hold with high probability and uniformly across locations and bandwidth matrices.

Uniformity makes the results relevant to more than the density estimate at a single chosen point. The authors apply their analysis to finding modes, estimating regions above a density threshold, and estimating class probabilities. For these applications, they obtain optimal convergence rates up to logarithmic factors, connecting a general estimation result to several downstream statistical tasks.

The paper also extends its results under the manifold hypothesis and establishes uniform convergence for estimating local intrinsic dimension. These additions bring the analysis to settings where the geometry of the data is itself relevant to estimation. The overall contribution is a collection of linked statistical guarantees: finite-sample control for KDE supports precise rates for derived quantities and extends to questions about underlying dimensional structure.
icml-2017-uniform-convergence-rates-for-.tldr: Uniform finite-sample KDE bounds yield near-optimal rates for several estimation tasks, with extensions to manifolds and local intrinsic dimension.

paragraphs: Sparse undirected graphical models describe interactions underlying discrete observations in areas such as biology and neuroscience. Bayesian inference is appealing for these problems, but doubly intractable Monte Carlo sampling makes it difficult to use. The paper develops a scalable variational framework through two complementary methods that address inference and sparsity.

Persistent VI handles discrete undirected models while avoiding doubly intractable MCMC and approximations of the partition function. Fadeout addresses variational inference with sparsity-inducing priors. It uses noncentered parameterizations to capture posterior correlations between model parameters and hyperparameters, preserving relationships relevant to learning which interactions are present.

Together, the methods substantially improve learning of sparse undirected graphical models in simulated and real problems from physics and biology. The two components tackle different parts of the challenge: performing inference in an undirected model and representing uncertainty under sparsity-promoting priors. Their combined empirical results support the framework as a practical route to Bayesian learning in settings where the usual sampling requirements have discouraged its use.
icml-2017-variational-inference-for-spar.tldr: Persistent VI and Fadeout combine scalable inference with sparsity-aware parameterization to improve Bayesian learning of undirected graphical models.
